newsitem.title: USA: New Mexico museum gathers O'Keeffe skulls, flowers.
newsitem.headline: New Mexico museum gathers O'Keeffe skulls, flowers.

text.p: Eleven years after the death of eccentric artist Georgia O'Keeffe, a long-awaited museum showcasing her stark landscape paintings of the American West opens this week in Santa Fe.

For years, visitors have come to this northern New Mexico town in search of O'Keeffe's huge floating skulls, erotic flowers and coral-coloured landscapes, but all they found were a few study pieces in museums and private collections.
That changes on Thursday when the new Georgia O'Keeffe Museum opens just off Santa Fe's famous downtown plaza with the world's largest permanent collection of her work.

Thousands of O'Keeffe fans are expected to attend the event and study paintings like the giant "Jimson Weed," which she painted in the courtyard of her home in the tiny village of Abiquiu 50 miles (80 km) northwest of here in 1932.
They will also come to learn more about O'Keeffe's rich and controversial life, which led her from the skyscrapers of New York to the badlands of northern New Mexico.

Peter Hassrick, director of the new museum, said they will not be disappointed. "This will satisfy the appetite and wonder of the most ardent fan," Hassrick said of the more than 80 O'Keeffe paintings, drawings and sculptures on display inside the museum's adobe walls.
O'Keeffe's fame has soared since her death in Santa Fe on March 6, 1986, at the age of 98.
The new museum is the dream of Anne Marion, a Texas philanthropist and avid O'Keeffe collector.

"It has always seemed unfortunate that there were not significant examples of her work able to be seen in this place she so personified," says Marion, who first envisaged an O'Keeffe museum when visiting Santa Fe as a child.

Marion's $200 million Burnett Foundation has donated the lion's share of the funding for the museum, which cost between $10 million and $15 million. Hollywood actor Gene Hackman, a mueseum board member and Santa Fe resident, will open the museum on Thursday.
O'Keeffe first came to New Mexico in 1917 and was immediately captivated by its landscapes. "I was always on my way back," she later recalled.
The state provided O'Keeffe with inspiration for paintings like "Ladder to the Moon," "Antelope" and "Black Hollyhock," which have been etched into the popular imagination of the U.S. Southwest.
Stanley Marcus, a museum adviser, calls the images of sparse, barren landscapes and sun-bleached skulls and bones the "killer O'Keeffes."

About 150,000 people are expected to visit the new museum this year. Every year, thousands of visitors wander through O'Keeffe's mud-floored home in Abiquiu, where she lived for nearly 40 years before moving to Santa Fe a couple of years before her death.
More than a dozen of her paintings have sold at public auction for more than $1 million during the last 10 years, and one of her paintings was recently sent to the White House.
Art critics and friends say O'Keeffe was an eccentric, reclusive figure who guarded her privacy fiercely and followed her goals with a single-minded determination.
She identified herself closely with her art. When a reporter once asked to speak to her for a moment, she gestured to her paintings and said: "Of course, just look around."

Marcus said the exhibitions had been designed using the guidelines O'Keeffe set for her own shows. He said O'Keeffe was at last receiving the type of recognition she deserved as one of America's great modernist painters.
"O'Keeffe is in a way a national treasure," said Marcus, owner-founder of the Neiman Marcus chain of department stores. "She was an American, an original."

Ellen Bradbury, a former director of the state Fine Arts Museum, first met O'Keeffe in the 1970s. She said the artist would have enjoyed the renewed attention the museum was attracting to her life and work.
"She liked being famous. I don't think she'd have given it up for the world," Bradbury said.
